back: The sinking of a denser oceanic plate beneath another plate into the mantle, where it melts.
Plates move apart; magma rises to form new crust; ridges and rift valleys; small shallow earthquakes and gentle eruptions. E.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift.
Oceanic plate subducted; trench, fold mountains or island arcs; strong earthquakes and explosive volcanoes. E.g. Nazca and South American plates (Andes).
Two continental plates push together and crumple into fold mountains; strong earthquakes, few or no volcanoes. E.g. Himalayas.
Plates slide past each other; crust neither made nor destroyed; earthquakes but no volcanoes. E.g. San Andreas Fault.
A plume of hot mantle rock beneath a plate, away from boundaries, forming a chain of volcanoes as the plate moves. E.g. Hawaii.
The belt of destructive boundaries around the Pacific Ocean with most of the world's active volcanoes and strongest earthquakes.
Continents drift through latitudes, mountains alter winds and rain, new seaways change ocean currents, and eruptions release ash and gases.
